videos.title: Why AI Has DHH Working 16-Hour Days
videos.description:
David Heinemeier Hansson thinks the agent era is reopening a window in computing that has been closed for decades: the chance to build a new operating system people actually want to use.

DHH joins a16z General Partners Martin Casado and Anish Acharya to explain why he’s building Omarchy, an agent-first Linux distribution designed around a computer that users can modify simply by asking.

They discuss why the command lines, config files, and detailed error messages that once made Linux intimidating now make it unusually well suited to agents, and why DHH believes software development has become cheap enough to challenge decades-old platform lock-in.

But if code is becoming abundant, what still matters? DHH argues that taste, craft, and the willingness to obsess over the final 2% become more important, not less. The conversation moves from tiny teams wielding the productive capacity of thousands of people to open models, competition at the frontier, and the return of hacker, demo, and pseudonymous internet culture.

videos.title: Coordinating Agents on Large-Scale Work with Cursor Projects
videos.description:
In this workshop, Aryaman Khandelwal, Product Manager, and Jon Grigull, Special Projects, at SpaceXSI, show how Cursor Projects lets one coordinator direct a fleet of agents on large-scale work, and how multiplayer Projects lets a whole team share that work, with a live look inside a real Project.

Key topics covered:
• From parallel agents to orchestration: Aryaman traces how AI coding moved from autocomplete and short back-and-forth turns, to running three to five agents in parallel, to Projects, where one coordinator plans the work and delegates it to workers that write the code.
• Multiplayer Projects and shared context: See how teammates each get their own coordinator in one Project, share a task board and a library of docs and artifacts, and let their coordinators message each other to sort out overlapping work before it turns into a merge conflict.
• A live look inside a Project: Watch Aryaman walk through the Agents pill, the task board, the shared library, and the PR panel, then start a new Project and connect the docs, task tracker, messaging app, and data sources it needs.
• Verification loops and environments: Aryaman explains how his team sets up environments, review rules, and how-we-work preferences so agents can test their own changes and open PRs that are ready for a person to review, and he shares his top advice for a first Project, which is to give it enough scope.

videos.title: The Boomerang CEO(s): With MongoDB’s Dev Ittycheria
videos.description:
Dev Ittycheria ran MongoDB for 11 years, took it from about $35 million in revenue to more than $2.3 billion, and retired. Ten months later his successor left, and within a week Dev was back in the chair. Since we recorded this, I’ve announced that I’m going back to HubSpot as CEO in addition to my work at Sequoia, so I’ve been replaying his advice with a lot more at stake.

The center of this conversation is Dev’s definition of the job, a framing he credits to former Palo Alto Networks CEO Mark McLaughlin. A CEO has three jobs: set the strategy, get the right people on the bus to execute it, and create an environment where they’re set up to win. A CEO can do a thousand things, and if they do 997 of them well and those three poorly, they’ve failed. Strategy doesn’t change that often, so most of the work is the second job: managing the team for the next stage. Dev also says the most challenging calls of being a CEO tested his courage more than his intelligence.

The time away sharpened all of it. Dev says distance let him see which issues really mattered and where he’d wasted time on little stuff. When he came back, he went straight to the team and made decisions quickly instead of dribbling them out.

We also get into why conflict-averse CEOs become the problem, how to hire a CRO, and the four things that have changed about the job in the AI era.

Those three jobs are the list I’m taking with me. Hopefully they’ll help you as well.

videos.title: AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI
videos.description:
This talk unpacks key insights from the third AI100 report, "AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI," released in November 2026. Commissioned by the AI100 standing committee and led by study panel chair Michael Wooldridge, the report documents what it calls the "scaling era" – the pivotal five years that reshaped how the world works with AI.

In this talk, you'll explore the report's findings across twelve standing questions and two deep dives, including:
• Advances in reasoning models and agentic systems
• The geopolitics of compute and data
• The contested evidence on AI's effects on work

The talk closes by revisiting the 2021 panel's predictions: asking why even the field's own insiders underestimated how far scaling the transformer would go, and what that reveals about our ability to forecast what comes next.

Recorded November 18, 2026 at Stanford University.


—

About AI100

The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is a longitudinal effort administered out of Stanford HAI and managed by a standing committee of AI experts from around the world, chaired by Sheila McIlraith, Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto. Its mission is to assess AI not as a snapshot, but as an evolving force across technical, ethical, economic, and societal domains. Every five years, we return to the same standing questions and answer them anew in a changed world.

videos.title: Turning Stranded Energy Into Intelligence: Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller
videos.description:
Chase Lochmiller runs one of the most operationally complex companies in AI: Crusoe builds power plants, manufactures electrical equipment, operates gigawatt-scale data centers, and runs a managed AI cloud on top, all under one roof. He just closed a round at a $31 billion valuation, and he got there by selling off the Bitcoin mining business that was paying the bills.

Chase explains why Crusoe is modeled on Exxon, not a cloud provider, and why he partners with companies that look like competitors. He makes the case that a company that outgrows the person who got it there is the rule, not the exception, and that CEOs almost always fire too slowly. He also talks candidly about hiring a coach, working hard to become a polished speaker when it didn’t come naturally, and why the data center industry’s biggest problem is a marketing problem.

I meet with a group of Sequoia founder CEOs between 20 and 2,000 employees, and one of them told me his business is becoming dizzyingly complex beneath him. Chase has the clearest answer I’ve heard for how to hold that in your head. 

And yes, we talk about summiting Everest.

videos.title: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) EXPLAINED | Everything Is a Plugin
videos.description:
In this video we take a deep dive into DeepSeek Harness (DSH), DeepSeek's open-source agent harness, built on the Cordis plugin system around one idea: everything is a plugin, including the agent loop, the tools, and even the system prompt.

We start with a quick tour of the new Electron desktop application, then break down the architecture of DSH and the history and design of Cordis, the plugin system that powers it. We look at how plugins provide services, how dependency injection and events connect every part of the application, and how Cordis tracks registrations to clean up plugins safely when they unmount.

Then we go hands-on: we write real plugins in code, run `dsh web --patch` with a custom `cordis.patch.yml`, watch three plugins (a greet tool, a bash guard, and a hello plugin) load and fire inside the app, and finish by loading the plugins into the desktop application via npm packages and the `.dsh` user configuration.

By the end, you'll understand how the composability of DSH works and how to create and load your own plugins, including a custom agent loop that never calls a model.

videos.title: AlphaGenome 2: Teaching AI to read the entire human genome
videos.description:
98% of human DNA doesn't build proteins—it controls how our cells work, and holds vital clues to why diseases happen and why 90% of new drugs fail in clinical trials. Understanding the genome at the molecular level is the key to deciphering the blueprint of human life.

In this episode, Professor Hannah Fry speaks with Google DeepMind's Žiga Avsec and Adam Gayoso about AlphaGenome, the AlphaGenome Atlas, and AlphaGenome 2—exploring how AI reads non-coding DNA down to single-cell resolution to pinpoint disease-causing mutations and help researchers solve medical mysteries.

Timecodes:
00:00 Introduction to AlphaGenome
04:01 Genotype, Phenotype & DNA
08:30 Transformers to AlphaGenome
12:11 Mapping the Genome 
17:45 Rare disease cases
21:10 AlphaGenome 2
30:06 Future vision 
38:45 Hannah's thoughts

Read more about AlphaGenome 2: https://deepmind.google/blog/alphagenome-2-deciphering-how-cells-read-dna-to-better-understand-disease/

videos.title: Confronting Our AI Future: The Speed of Intelligence
videos.description:
This panel tracks how quickly AI's capability is advancing, the security and safety questions that come with moving this fast, and the hardware race underpinning all of it. The panelists offer a rare combination of research, security, and infrastructure perspectives on what it actually takes to keep pushing the frontier forward.

*Speakers:*

- Yejin Choi: Dieter Schwarz Foundation Professor of Computer Science at Stanford University and a Senior Fellow at Stanford HAI. Her research centers on democratizing generative AI — building smaller yet powerful language models, scaling intelligence through smarter algorithms and alternative training recipes, pluralistic alignment, and AI for science and social good.

- Dawn Song: Professor in Computer Science at UC Berkeley and Co-Director of Berkeley Center for Responsible Decentralized Intelligence. Her research interest lies in AI safety and security, Agentic AI, deep learning, security and privacy, and decentralization technology. 

- Andrew Feldman: Cerebras Co-founder, Chief Executive Officer, President & Chairman of the Board. He has previously held positions at AMD, SeaMicro (acquired by ADM), and Force 10 Networks (acquired by Dell). 

- Ryan McMorrow (Moderator): West Coast Finance Correspondent at Financial Times.

_Confronting Our AI Future: Hope, Fear, and the Choices Ahead_ is a Stanford HAI conference examining the anxiety that AI's rapid acceleration has raised for students, workers, and leaders, and the choices that will shape what comes next. It took place on October 28, 2026, on the Stanford campus.
